title: Secured Personal Loan Costs and Collateral Rules
metaDescription: Learn how a secured personal loan works and what happens to your collateral if you cannot repay the balance.
cardBlurb: How pledging an asset lowers your borrowing rate and the specific risks you take on if you stop making payments.
introText:
A secured personal loan requires you to pledge an asset as collateral to guarantee repayment. Because the lender's risk drops, you typically get a lower interest rate than with an unsecured loan.

At ModernWallet, we show the math, name what moves it, and explain the tradeoff. Pledging collateral can make approval easier when your credit score sits below conventional lending standards. The risk is direct. You surrender ownership rights to your pledged property if you fail to pay down the balance.

sections.heading: How a Secured Personal Loan Operates
sections.body:
A secured personal loan functions as a fixed-rate installment contract backed by a specific personal asset that the lender holds as a security interest.

According to the [Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/personal-loans/), an unsecured loan relies entirely on your credit history, while a secured loan gives the lender a direct claim against your collateral. Because the lending institution holds this backstop, you can often qualify for a lower annual percentage rate (APR). You may also secure a larger loan balance than an unsecured approval would provide.

Lenders view collateral as insurance against loss. This safety net allows banks and credit unions to approve your application if you lack an established credit file. You trade your asset's security for better loan terms. Before you apply, you can run potential loan terms through our [personal loan calculator](/personal-loan/) to see how different interest rates shape your monthly obligations.

sections.heading: Collateral Options from Savings Accounts to Vehicles
sections.body:
You can pledge several asset classes as loan security, ranging from cash deposits to physical property you own outright.

The lowest-risk structure for you is often a share-secured loan or savings-secured loan. Guidance from [MyCreditUnion.gov](https://mycreditunion.gov/manage-your-money/consumer-loans-credit-cards) explains that this arrangement uses funds already sitting in your credit union share account or personal savings account as collateral. A certificate-secured loan operates the same way using a certificate of deposit (CD). The financial institution places a freeze on your pledged amount, preventing you from withdrawing those funds. Your money does not sit idle. Your pledged savings continue earning interest or credit union dividends while you repay the borrowed funds. Because the lender already controls this cash, the institution calculates your loan rate as a simple margin above your deposit yield rather than pricing off your credit score.

You can also pledge a vehicle that you own free and clear of existing liens. Using your car as collateral is distinct from an initial purchase loan, but the operational danger remains identical. If you stop paying, the lender can take the car. High-cost products like car title loans and pawn transactions also demand collateral, but they belong to an entirely different borrowing category. The CFPB cautions that title lenders can charge annual rates far above a standard personal loan; confirm the current rate on any title lender's own page before signing. Standard personal loans from mainstream institutions avoid those predatory rate structures.

sections.heading: Default Consequences and Property Seizure
sections.body:
Defaulting on a secured personal loan allows the lender to seize and liquidate your pledged collateral without obtaining a prior court judgment.

When you sign a secured agreement, you grant the lender a voluntary lien. Under CFPB lending rules, that legal lien permits the lender to repossess your pledged vehicle or absorb your frozen bank funds as soon as you breach the contract terms. An unsecured lender lacks that direct shortcut. To collect on an unsecured balance, a lender must sue you in civil court, obtain a formal judgment, and seek wage garnishment or a bank levy. A secured creditor skips the courtroom entirely.

If you pledge a savings balance, the credit union simply transfers your cash to cover your unpaid principal and interest. If you pledge a vehicle, a repossession agent can tow your car from your driveway. Loss of the asset is not always the end of your obligation. If your liquidated property sells for less than your remaining loan balance, you still owe that remaining deficiency. You can track how pledged assets alter your overall financial standing by using our [net worth calculator](/net-worth/).

sections.heading: Comparing a Secured Personal Loan to Unsecured Rates
sections.body:
Comparing a secured personal loan against an unsecured loan reveals that collateral backing yields major interest savings if your credit score falls into fair or poor bands.

Unsecured personal loan pricing tracks your credit profile closely. Benchmark data from [Experian](https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/best-personal-loan-rates/) shows how unsecured average APR offers break down across standard tiers:
If your credit score is 760 or higher, you can expect rates from 7% to 10%.
At 720 to 759, you average 10% to 14%.
At 680 to 719, you average 14% to 20%.
At 640 to 679, you average 20% to 28%.
Below 640, you face average rates climbing between 26% and 36%.

To track broader borrowing trends across the wider market, the [Federal Reserve](https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/current/) publishes its G.19 Consumer Credit report as a lender-independent pricing benchmark. Because share-secured loans price off your deposit yield instead of your credit score, you might qualify for a 6% APR even if your credit score sits in a subprime band.

Look at the numbers on a $5,000 borrowing need over a 36-month repayment term. If you take an unsecured loan at a 28% APR, your monthly payment comes to $206.82. That loan costs you $2,445.45 in total interest over three years. If you use a credit union savings account to back a secured loan at 6% APR over that same 36-month timeline, your monthly payment drops to $152.11. Your total interest drops to $475.96. Choosing the secured path lowers your monthly outlay by $54.71. You save exactly $1,969.50 in total interest charges. Explore our guide on [secured vs. unsecured loan](/compare/secured-vs-unsecured-loan/) tradeoffs to evaluate which debt structure fits your current balance sheet.

sections.heading: Secured Personal Loan Rules vs Revolving Credit Cards
sections.body:
A secured personal loan delivers a single lump-sum payout with fixed monthly installment payments, whereas a secured credit card provides an open-ended revolving line of credit.

Consumer guidance from the [National Credit Union Administration (NCUA)](https://ncua.gov/consumers) highlights how product structures serve different financial needs. With a secured credit card, you supply a refundable security deposit that dictates your spending limit. You make repeat purchases, pay off your monthly statement, and borrow repeatedly without submitting a new application. A secured personal loan disburses the entire proceeds to you upfront. You pay down the balance through identical monthly installments over a set schedule of two to five years.

If your objective is building a credit history through routine daily purchases, a secured credit card is the more practical tool. If you need a specific sum to handle an expense and want a guaranteed payoff date, an installment loan makes more sense. You can calculate how extra principal contributions shorten your debt timeline by testing our [personal loan extra payment calculator](/personal-loan/extra-payment-calculator/).

sections.heading: Situations Where Pledging Collateral Fails
sections.body:
You should avoid taking out a secured loan if the pledged property is needed for your daily commute or employment.

This borrowing method is not for you if you cannot afford to lose the underlying asset. If you pledge the sole vehicle you rely on to commute to your job, an unexpected layoff puts your transportation at risk. Losing your car can lead directly to losing your income. Similarly, if you already maintain excellent credit qualifying you for a single-digit unsecured rate, pledging collateral provides little financial upside. You would take on unnecessary default risk to shave a fraction of a percent off your rate. If your monthly budget is already stretched thin, do not gamble property you depend on daily to secure cash. Review your household numbers with our [budget calculator](/budget/) before committing to any collateral pledge.

sections.heading: Conditions That Flip the Financing Choice
sections.body:
Our recommendation flips against a secured loan when the interest rate gap between secured and unsecured offers narrows to less than two percentage points.

If an unsecured lender offers you a loan at 9% APR and a credit union offers a share-secured loan at 7.5% APR, the rate difference is only 1.5 percentage points. On a $3,000 loan over 24 months, that spread amounts to less than $50 in total interest savings. Saving $50 does not justify locking up $3,000 of your liquid emergency cash or signing away repossession rights to your vehicle.

Our recommendation also flips if you plan to pay off the entire debt within several months. Rapid prepayment reduces the total interest you accrue, rendering the secured rate discount negligible. Finally, verify current rates directly with prospective lenders. Rates for specific products change frequently and remain unpublished until lenders evaluate your individual application profile.

sections.heading: Action Steps Before Pledging Your Assets
sections.body:
Before you pledge collateral to any lender, determine the replacement value of your asset and obtain a prequalification quote for an unsecured alternative.

Request written terms that state whether the lender charges prepayment penalties or documentation fees. For a share-secured agreement, confirm that your locked deposit balance continues to earn its regular interest rate throughout the loan term. Compare the total repayment cost of both borrowing paths side by side. Once you confirm that the interest savings justify the asset risk, you can finalize your secured personal loan application with clear expectations.

faqs.question: What is a secured personal loan?
faqs.answer: A secured personal loan is an installment loan backed by an asset you own, such as savings or a vehicle, which the lender can take if you do not pay. The CFPB notes that this collateral reduces the lender's default risk, which generally helps you qualify for lower interest rates and higher borrowing amounts than an unsecured loan offers.

faqs.question: What can I use as collateral for a personal loan?
faqs.answer: You can use cash in a savings account, a certificate of deposit, or a vehicle that you own outright as collateral. Credit unions frequently offer share-secured loans that place a temporary hold on your savings while allowing your funds to keep earning interest. Pledging home equity is also possible, though it is less common for a basic personal loan.

faqs.question: What happens if I default on a secured personal loan?
faqs.answer: The lender can seize and liquidate your pledged collateral without filing a lawsuit or winning a court judgment first. According to CFPB rules, your loan agreement gives the lender an automatic security interest in the property. If the sale of the asset does not cover your remaining balance, the lender may pursue you for the remaining deficiency.

faqs.question: Is a secured personal loan cheaper than an unsecured one?
faqs.answer: Yes, a secured personal loan is almost always cheaper than an unsecured loan from the same financial institution. Because the lender holds collateral to recover its funds, interest rates are lower. If you have fair or poor credit, a share-secured loan priced at a modest margin over deposit yields can save you thousands of dollars in interest compared to a high unsecured APR.

faqs.question: Is a secured personal loan the same as a secured credit card?
faqs.answer: No, they are structured differently. A secured personal loan delivers a single lump-sum payout that you repay in fixed monthly installments over a set term. A secured credit card provides an open-ended revolving credit line backed by a cash security deposit, designed for ongoing purchases and balance management.

faqs.question: Are car title loans a good way to get a secured personal loan?
faqs.answer: No, car title loans are predatory products that charge excessive interest rates and should be avoided. The CFPB warns that title lenders hold your vehicle title as collateral and can charge annual rates far above a standard personal loan; check the lender's own disclosure for the actual rate. A standard secured personal loan from a bank or credit union charges standard market rates and protects your rights.
